newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Now coffee tops $3 per pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Now coffee tops $3 per pound.

text.p: A spectacular rally in coffee prices accelerated on Thursday to lift New York futures above $3 per pound for the first time in 20 years.
London prices for the less-prized robusta beans couldn't match a gain of 150 percent since January on the arabica types that are traded in New York.
Even so, they put on almost 20 percent in just a few wild hours of buying to rise above $2,650 per tonne. This was 120 percent higher than where they began 1997.
The rally is unprecedented in that there hasn't - yet - been a winter frost in Brazil this year. Coffee is up because of tight Latin American supply and low stocks.
Against that backdrop, the onset about now of the season of the year when Brazil may get a damaging frost, has been enough to trigger a frenzy of speculative buying.
"Speculators have been piling into coffee ahead of the frost season in Brazil," brokerage GNI Ltd said in a monthly report.

Should a severe frost hit Brazil "then coffee prices could soar to $5, perhaps $7 per pound," it said. "But if a frost is not seen, the downside for prices could perhaps be $1.50 or so. It seems like a fair bet."
The benchmark New York July arabica contract hit $3.15 per pound, up almost 20 cents from Wednesday, before profit-takers took a few cents of the froth off the top of the market.
Latest data in Tokyo meanwhile showed a jump of 13.5 percent in April coffee imports by Japan as roasters there scrambled to buy coffee in the tight world market.
Douwe Egberts in the Netherlands, with a hike of 30 cents on a standard pack, on Thursday became the latest in a line of retailers to levy new increases in the shops in the United States and Europe.

"This is an historic moment - but also a worrying one. These prices could start to hit consumption as housewives may start buying smaller quantities," says Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association.
The view among traders in Brazil is that hitting the $3 mark may bring some profit-taking to the futures arena, but that prices could pick up again afterwards on concern about the risk of a frost.
After September, however, if there is a frost-free winter, they are likely to slip towards $2 and lower, as supplies from Central America come in.
Other commodity markets could not match the excitement in coffee on Thursday.
The price of gold was itself stubbornly unmoved amid the turmoil over what Germany does with its bullion reserves. It fixed in London at $343.90 an ounce which was up from $342.80 on Wednesday.

But dealers were unsure how much that reflected news late Wednesday that the Bundesbank rejected a government plan to revalue German reserves, to use the paper profit to plug gaps in the 1997 budget and bring Germany within criteria for European Monetary Union.

Andy Smith, bullion analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland, said the German row could be positive for gold, against a backdrop of present fears that European central banks may sell metal to meet EMU rules.
EMU might be postponed, or go ahead on the basis that balance sheets would be massaged. Either way "the need for gold sales is reduced..." Smith said.
Palladium hit a new record high official price on Thursday at $196 an ounce, on Russian supply concerns in what continues to be a very tight market.
Crude oil fell then recovered after the latest energy data from the United States showed the world's biggest consumer was well stocked with crude oil and oil products last week.
The marker Brent Blend from the North Sea for July delivery traded down to a low of $19.10 a barrel before bouncing back towards $19.40.
